commands.name: monitor
commands.short: Monitor uptime, SSL certificates and domain expiry, and manage incidents and alerts
commands.long:
Norcube Monitor checks your sites, certificates and domains on a schedule
from Norcube's servers. A monitor is an HTTP check (optionally with a
keyword), an SSL certificate check or a domain expiry check. Problems
confirmed by consecutive checks open incidents, which alert through your
alert channels (email, webhook, Slack, Discord, SMS). Status pages show
chosen monitors to the public. Maintenance windows pause alerts for planned
work and keep it out of uptime.

Monitors and channels are named by their id or, where a command says so,
by their exact name. Checks count towards your Norcube Monitor usage, on a
schedule and when you run one now.

In CI, "monitor status --fail-on critical" fails the job while a
critical incident is open, and "monitor monitors run <monitor> --wait"
fails it when the check finds the monitor down. CI tokens need a
Norcube Monitor scope: monitor.read (everything that reads),
monitor.check (run checks), monitor.write (manage monitors and
incidents), monitor.channels (manage alert channels),
monitor.statuspages (manage status pages, post on them and manage their
subscribers) or monitor.maintenance (manage maintenance windows; one that
shows on a published page also takes monitor.statuspages). monitor.write
includes none of the last three.

commands.name: channels
commands.short: Manage alert channels: email, webhooks, Slack, Discord and SMS
commands.long:
Alert channels are where incidents alert. Default channels get the
alerts of every monitor that follows the organization's defaults; a
monitor's own routes ("monitors alerts set") name channels directly.

Credentials stay secret: Slack and Discord URLs are read from a file or
standard input and shown only as a hint, and a webhook's signing secret is
written to a file you name, never printed. Email-address and SMS channels
get no alerts until their contact confirms a code ("channels verify").
A CI token changes channels only with the monitor.channels scope
(monitor.write doesn't include it); any Norcube Monitor scope reads them.

commands.name: create
commands.short: Create an alert channel
commands.long:
Creates a channel of one kind:

  email    --address (confirmed with a code sent there) or --members
  webhook  --url; signed with a secret Norcube Monitor generates (saved with
           --secret-file, never printed) or yours (--signing-secret-file)
  slack    --url-file: the incoming-webhook URL, from a file or stdin
  discord  --url-file: the webhook URL, from a file or stdin
  sms      --phone (confirmed with a code texted there)

Email-address and SMS channels get no alerts until verified: run
"channels verify <channel>" (on a terminal it asks for the code).
commands.example:
norcube monitor channels create "Ops" --kind email --address ops@example.com --default
norcube monitor channels create "On-call webhook" --kind webhook --url https://example.com/hooks/monitor --secret-file webhook-secret.txt
pbpaste | norcube monitor channels create "#alerts" --kind slack --url-file -
norcube monitor channels create "On-call phone" --kind sms --phone +420601123456

and phone numbers removed. --status dead lists the failures nobody saw.

commands.name: test
commands.short: Send a test alert through a channel now
commands.long:
Sends a test alert right away and prints the provider's reference. Rate
limited (20 per user and 60 per organization an hour); an SMS counts
toward the daily SMS limit, so SMS channels ask first (--yes skips it).
commands.example: norcube monitor channels test "On-call webhook"

commands.name: update
commands.short: Rename, enable, disable or reconfigure an alert channel
commands.long:
Changes only what you pass. New settings replace the kind's settings as a
whole (a Slack or Discord URL must be given again); a new address or phone
number needs verifying again. --rotate-secret gives a webhook a new
signing secret, written to --secret-file.
commands.example:
norcube monitor channels update "Ops" --default=false
norcube monitor channels update "On-call webhook" --rotate-secret --secret-file new-secret.txt
norcube monitor channels update "On-call phone" --phone +420601999888

commands.name: verify
commands.short: Confirm an SMS or email-address channel with the code sent to it
commands.long:
Email-address and SMS channels get no alerts until their contact
confirms a 6-digit code (valid 10 minutes, 5 attempts).

On a terminal, verify sends a code and asks for it. In a script, run it
once to send the code, then again with --code-file (- reads standard
input) to confirm. The code is never taken as an argument nor printed.
A new code can be sent after a minute (--resend), at most 5 a day.
commands.example:
norcube monitor channels verify "On-call phone"
norcube monitor channels verify 0c2d4f6a-8b1e-4c3d-9e5f-7a6b5c4d3e2f --resend
echo 123456 | norcube monitor channels verify 0c2d4f6a-8b1e-4c3d-9e5f-7a6b5c4d3e2f --code-file -

commands.name: incidents
commands.short: List, inspect and acknowledge incidents
commands.long:
An incident is a confirmed problem with one aspect of a monitor: its
availability, its certificate or its domain. It opens after the monitor's
confirmations (or at once for an expiry), alerts the monitor's channels,
reminds until acknowledged, and resolves when the checks are good again.

commands.name: acknowledge
commands.short: Acknowledge an incident: someone is on it, stop the reminders
commands.long: Marks an open incident as being handled; its reminders stop. Idempotent: a resolved or already acknowledged incident is returned unchanged.
commands.example: norcube monitor incidents acknowledge 3f2c8a8e-6c1d-4a59-9a43-2b1f0f6f9d10

commands.name: get
commands.short: Show an incident with its timeline and the alerts sent
commands.long:
Shows the incident, its timeline (opened, escalated, reminders,
acknowledged, resolved) and every alert sent for it with its delivery
status, so a failing channel shows here.
commands.example:
norcube monitor incidents get 3f2c8a8e-6c1d-4a59-9a43-2b1f0f6f9d10
norcube monitor incidents get 3f2c8a8e-6c1d-4a59-9a43-2b1f0f6f9d10 -o json --query timeline

commands.name: list
commands.short: List incidents, open ones first
commands.long:
Lists incidents: open critical ones first, then open warnings, then
resolved ones, newest first within each. Every filter given must match.
--severity reads an open incident's current severity and a resolved one's
peak, so "--severity critical" finds every incident that ever paged.
--since and --until select by when the incident started.
commands.example:
norcube monitor incidents list --status open
norcube monitor incidents list --status open --unacknowledged --severity critical
norcube monitor incidents list --monitor "Shop" --since 30d -o json

commands.name: summary
commands.short: Count open incidents by severity, and resolved ones with the time to resolve
commands.long:
The organization's incidents at a glance: open ones by current severity
and those nobody acknowledged, incidents resolved in the last 7 and 30
days, and the mean time from opened to resolved over the last 30 days.
For a pass or fail answer in CI use "monitor status --fail-on".
commands.example:
norcube monitor incidents summary
norcube monitor incidents summary -o json --query open.critical

commands.name: maintenance
commands.short: Schedule maintenance windows that pause alerts and stay out of uptime
commands.long:
A maintenance window is planned work on monitors or status page components.
While it runs, its monitors don't alert or open incidents for availability
problems, and the time stays out of their uptime. Checks keep running and
count towards your usage. A certificate or domain running out still alerts,
because that is true whatever work is going on.

A window shows by itself on every published status page displaying one of its
targets, and subscribers get mail when it is scheduled, starts and finishes
unless you turn that off. Which pages show it isn't a choice: otherwise a page
could stay green while its alerts are silent.

A CI token changes windows with the monitor.maintenance scope, and also needs
monitor.statuspages when a window shows on a published page. Cancelling or
finishing needs only monitor.maintenance, so whoever can edit a window can
always end its silence. Any Norcube Monitor scope reads them.

A window ends by itself, so a deploy that dies before "finish" can't silence
alerts for longer than you asked for. Wrap a deploy in one:

  id=$(norcube monitor maintenance create --monitor api --title "Deploy" --duration 15m -o id)
  ./deploy.sh
  norcube monitor maintenance finish "$id"

commands.name: cancel
commands.short: Call off a maintenance window that hasn't started
commands.long:
Calls off a scheduled window. It won't run, and subscribers who were told hear
it was cancelled. One that has started exits 8: use "finish" instead. It needs
only the monitor.maintenance scope, even on a published page.
commands.example:
norcube monitor maintenance cancel 4d3c2b1a-0f9e-4d8c-b7a6-5f4e3d2c1b0a
norcube monitor maintenance cancel 4d3c2b1a-0f9e-4d8c-b7a6-5f4e3d2c1b0a --yes

flags.name: yes
flags.description: Don't ask for confirmation

commands.name: create
commands.short: Schedule a maintenance window, or start one now
commands.long:
Schedules a window. Without --start it begins right away. It needs a title,
at least one target, and --end or --duration; it can last at most 30 days and
start at most a year ahead.

It shows by itself on every published status page displaying a target, and
subscribers get all three mails unless you turn them off with --notify-scheduled,
--notify-started, --notify-finished or --no-notify. A window that starts within
15 minutes sends no scheduled mail, only the started one.

A CI token needs the monitor.maintenance scope, and monitor.statuspages too when
the window shows on a published page.
commands.example:
# Silence a monitor around a deploy
id=$(norcube monitor maintenance create --monitor api --title "Deploy" --duration 15m -o id)
./deploy.sh
norcube monitor maintenance finish "$id"

# Announce work for tomorrow on everything a status page shows
norcube monitor maintenance create --status-page acme --title "Database upgrade" --description "Short interruptions are expected." --start 2026-11-07T14:00:00Z --end 2026-11-07T16:00:00Z

# A quiet window nobody hears about
norcube monitor maintenance create --monitor "Shop API" --monitor "Shop cert" --title "Load test" --start +1h --duration 2h --no-notify

commands.name: finish
commands.short: End a maintenance window in progress now
commands.long:
Ends a window in progress. The next check counts and alerts as usual, monitors
with an open incident it held are checked again within a minute, and subscribers
hear it finished early. One that hasn't started exits 8: use "cancel" instead.

It asks for no confirmation, because ending a silence is the safe direction and
it has to run unattended at the end of a deploy. It needs only the
monitor.maintenance scope, even on a published page.
commands.example:
norcube monitor maintenance finish 4d3c2b1a-0f9e-4d8c-b7a6-5f4e3d2c1b0a
norcube monitor maintenance finish "$id"

commands.short: List maintenance windows, latest start first
commands.long: Lists the organization's windows, latest start first; with --state scheduled, soonest first.
commands.example:
norcube monitor maintenance list
norcube monitor maintenance list --state in_progress
norcube monitor maintenance list --monitor "Shop API" --all-pages
norcube monitor maintenance list --status-page acme --state scheduled -o json

commands.name: update
commands.short: Change a maintenance window, as far as where it stands allows
commands.long:
Changes only what you pass.

Before the window starts, everything can change; moving a time by 5 minutes or
more tells subscribers who were already told. Once it has started, its targets
and start are frozen: you can still change the text and the mail switches, and
extend or shorten it, which sends no mail. Once it is over, only the text can
change. A cancelled window can't change. The API refuses anything else with
exit 8.

--monitor, --component and --status-page replace the targets as a whole, so name
everything the window should keep. --duration counts from the new --start, or
else from the window's current start.

A CI token needs the monitor.maintenance scope, and monitor.statuspages too when
the window shows on a published page before or after the change. To end a window
now, use "finish"; to call off one that hasn't started, use "cancel".
commands.example:
# The deploy needs longer
norcube monitor maintenance update 4d3c2b1a-0f9e-4d8c-b7a6-5f4e3d2c1b0a --end +1h
norcube monitor maintenance update 4d3c2b1a-0f9e-4d8c-b7a6-5f4e3d2c1b0a --start 2026-11-08T14:00:00Z --duration 2h
norcube monitor maintenance update 4d3c2b1a-0f9e-4d8c-b7a6-5f4e3d2c1b0a --title "Database upgrade" --no-notify

commands.name: monitors
commands.short: Create, inspect and manage monitors and their check history
commands.long:
A monitor checks one thing on a schedule: an HTTP endpoint (optionally
for a keyword), an SSL certificate, or a domain's registration. Commands
that take a <monitor> accept its id or its exact name.

commands.name: alerts
commands.short: Where and when a monitor alerts
commands.long:
A monitor either follows the organization's defaults (its default
channels, or the members by email when none is default) or has its own
routes: which events go to which channels, how many failed checks open an
incident, how many good ones resolve it, and how often to remind.

commands.name: get
commands.short: Show how a monitor alerts
commands.example: norcube monitor monitors alerts get "Shop"

commands.name: set
commands.short: Set where and when a monitor alerts
commands.long:
Replaces the monitor's alerting. --defaults returns it to the
organization's defaults. Otherwise give its routes, each a channel (id or
exact name) and the events it gets (down, warning, expiring, expired,
recovered), or --mute for no alerts; settings you leave out keep their
current values. Channels themselves are managed with "monitor channels".
commands.example:
norcube monitor monitors alerts set "Shop" --route "On-call webhook=down,recovered" --route ops-email=down
norcube monitor monitors alerts set "Shop" --confirm-failures 3 --reminder 30m
norcube monitor monitors alerts set "Shop" --mute
norcube monitor monitors alerts set "Shop" --defaults

flags.name: confirm-successes

flags.description: Follow the organization's default channels again

flags.description: Read the API's alert settings body as JSON from this file (- for standard input)

flags.name: mute
flags.description: Send no alerts for this monitor

flags.name: reminder
flags.description: Remind about an unacknowledged critical incident this often, e.g. 1h (0 for no reminders)

flags.name: route

commands.name: availability
commands.short: A monitor's uptime and downtime per day

commands.name: get
commands.short: Show uptime and estimated downtime per UTC day
commands.long:
One row per UTC day ending today, oldest first: check counts, uptime and
an estimate of the minutes spent down (HTTP monitors). A day without
checks has no uptime, never 100%.
commands.example: norcube monitor monitors availability get "Shop" --days 30

flags.name: days
flags.description: Days ending today, 1 to 90 (default 90)

commands.name: bulk
commands.short: Pause, resume or delete many monitors at once
commands.long:
Applies one action to many monitors: the ones you name (ids or exact
names, as arguments or one per line with --file), or every monitor the
list filters match (--type, --status, --search). Each monitor is handled as
its own request would be, so one refusal doesn't stop the others; the
result lists every monitor with ok or its problem code. The command exits
1 when any monitor failed.

For planned work, "monitor maintenance create" is usually better than
pausing: checks keep running, the time stays out of uptime, status pages say
so, and it ends by itself.

commands.name: delete
commands.short: Delete many monitors and their history
commands.example:
norcube monitor monitors bulk delete 7d1c2f7e-6a1f-4f5e-9b8a-1f7c2b3d4e5f "Old landing page"
norcube monitor monitors bulk delete --file old-monitors.txt --yes

commands.name: pause
commands.short: Pause many monitors
commands.example:
# Pause everything behind api.example.com; for planned work, see "monitor maintenance"
norcube monitor monitors bulk pause --search api.example.com --yes

commands.name: certificate
commands.short: The newest TLS certificate an SSL or HTTPS monitor saw

commands.name: get
commands.short: Show the monitor's newest certificate and when it expires
commands.long:
Shows the newest certificate the monitor's checks saw: subject, issuer,
names, validity, whether the chain and hostname verify, and days left. SSL
monitors add the expiry thresholds and the next one to be crossed. Exits 3
when no check has seen a certificate (plain HTTP and domain monitors).
commands.example:
norcube monitor monitors certificate get "API cert"
norcube monitor monitors cert get "Shop" -o json --query certificate.notAfter

commands.name: create
commands.short: Create a monitor; its first check runs right away
commands.long:
Creates an enabled monitor of one type:

  http     requests --url and expects --expect (default 2xx) within --timeout;
           for https URLs it also watches the certificate and the domain's
           registration unless --no-cert-watch / --no-domain-watch
  keyword  an HTTP monitor that also looks for --keyword in the body
           (--keyword-mode absent: alerts when it appears)
  ssl      checks the certificate of --host:--port and alerts --alert-days
           before it expires
  domain   checks the registration of --domain and alerts --alert-days
           before it expires

Settings not given start from the dashboard's defaults. For anything the
flags don't cover, pass the API's JSON body with --from-file (see "nrc api
monitor POST /monitors"). Secret header values come from a file or
standard input only (--secret-headers-file), never from arguments. The
first check runs at once and is billed like a scheduled one.
commands.example:
norcube monitor monitors create "Shop" --type http --url https://shop.example.com/health
norcube monitor monitors create "Login page" --type keyword --url https://example.com/login --keyword "Sign in"
norcube monitor monitors create "API cert" --type ssl --host api.example.com --alert-days 30,7
norcube monitor monitors create "example.com" --type domain --domain example.com --interval 24h
printf 'Authorization: Bearer %s\n' "$TOKEN" | norcube monitor monitors create "Admin API" --type http --url https://example.com/admin/health --secret-headers-file -
norcube monitor monitors create --from-file monitor.json

commands.name: delete
commands.short: Delete a monitor and its whole check history
commands.long:
Deletes the monitor with its results, status history and incidents.
To stop checks but keep the history, use "monitors pause". A monitor that
belongs to another Norcube product (a DomainRadar saved domain's expiry
alerts) can't be deleted here (exit 8): remove it in that product.
commands.example:
norcube monitor monitors delete "Old landing page"
norcube monitor monitors delete 7d1c2f7e-6a1f-4f5e-9b8a-1f7c2b3d4e5f --yes

flags.description: Don't ask for confirmation

commands.name: get
commands.short: Show a monitor's settings and current status
commands.long: Shows the monitor, its check settings (secret header values are never returned), its status with the reason, and the certificate and domain it watches.
commands.example:
norcube monitor monitors get "Shop API"
norcube monitor monitors get 7d1c2f7e-6a1f-4f5e-9b8a-1f7c2b3d4e5f -o json

commands.name: list
commands.short: List monitors with their current status
commands.long:
Lists the organization's monitors, by default the ones that need
attention first (critical, warning, pending, ok, paused, then by name).
--status filters by the overall status: the worse of the monitor's own
status and the certificate and domain it watches.
commands.example:
norcube monitor monitors list
norcube monitor monitors list --status critical --type http
norcube monitor monitors list --search shop --sort uptime --all-pages -o json

commands.name: pause
commands.short: Stop a monitor's scheduled checks
commands.long:
Stops scheduled checks; the history stays. Pausing closes the monitor's
open incident without alerting. Idempotent.
commands.example: norcube monitor monitors pause "Shop API"

commands.name: results
commands.short: A monitor's check results

commands.name: list

commands.long:
Lists the monitor's checks in [--since, --until), newest first; by default
the last 24 hours. Raw results are kept at least 30 days. JSON has every
detail of a result: timings, the certificate seen, the domain's
registration.
commands.example:
norcube monitor monitors results list "Shop"
norcube monitor monitors results list "Shop" --since 7d --all-pages -o json --query "[?severity=='critical'].checkedAt"

commands.name: resume
commands.short: Restart a paused monitor's scheduled checks
commands.long:
Restarts scheduled checks; the next one runs right away unless the last
one is less than an interval old. Idempotent.
commands.example: norcube monitor monitors resume "Shop API"

commands.name: run
commands.short: Run a monitor's check now and show the result
commands.long:
Runs the monitor's check right away (paused monitors too) and prints the
stored result. The check is billed like a scheduled one and rate limited
(200 per user and 600 per organization an hour).

The check runs while the command waits, so the result is always final.
--wait makes the result the command's outcome, for deploy pipelines: it
exits 1 with code job_failed (the result in "details") when the check
found the monitor critical or couldn't reach a verdict (inconclusive), or
with --fail-on warning also when it found a warning, and prints nothing
on stdout then; it exits 7 when no result arrives within --wait-timeout. Without --wait the command exits 0
whatever the check found.

A maintenance window doesn't change any of that: --wait still fails on a
critical result, because it is there to tell whether the deploy worked. The
result says inMaintenance when one held the monitor.
commands.example:
norcube monitor monitors run "Shop API"
# Fail a deploy when the site is down after it
norcube monitor monitors run "Shop API" --wait
norcube monitor monitors run 7d1c2f7e-6a1f-4f5e-9b8a-1f7c2b3d4e5f --wait --fail-on warning -o json

flags.name: fail-on
flags.description: With --wait, the severity that fails the command: critical (default) or warning (inconclusive always fails)

flags.name: wait
flags.description: Wait until the check finishes (Ctrl-C stops waiting, not the check)

flags.name: wait-timeout
flags.description: Give up waiting after this long (the job keeps running on the server)

commands.name: stats
commands.short: A monitor's uptime and response times

commands.name: get
commands.short: Show uptime, response times and check counts over a range
commands.long:
Shows uptime ((ok + warning) / conclusive checks, HTTP monitors only),
average and maximum response time and check counts for the range ending
now. JSON adds the series: hourly buckets up to 7d, daily beyond.
Refreshed every few minutes.
commands.example:
norcube monitor monitors stats get "Shop"
norcube monitor monitors stats get "Shop" --range 30d -o json --query uptimePercent

commands.name: list

commands.long:
Lists each time a check moved the monitor to another status: from, to,
when, how long it lasted (the newest one is still going) and what the
check said. Kept a year. Pausing is not a status change. JSON adds the
events in each span (a renewed certificate).

norcube monitor monitors status-changes list "Shop"
norcube monitor monitors history list "Shop" -o json

commands.name: status
commands.short: Show the organization's monitoring status, or fail a CI job on open incidents
commands.long:
Shows the open incidents by severity, the monitors by status, and every
monitor that is critical or warning. The verdict ("status" in JSON) comes
from open incidents, which are problems the checks confirmed: critical
while a critical incident is open, warning while only warnings are, else
ok.

--fail-on turns the verdict into the exit code: with --fail-on critical
the command exits 1 (code unhealthy, the report in the error's details)
while a critical incident is open, with --fail-on warning while any
incident is open. The report is printed either way. The default, none,
always exits 0.

An incident a maintenance window holds doesn't count towards the verdict or
--fail-on, and its monitor moves from "problems" to "maintenance". A certificate
or domain running out isn't held: it stays in "problems" and still counts.
commands.example:
norcube monitor status
# Gate a deploy on Norcube Monitor
norcube monitor status --fail-on critical
norcube monitor status -o json --query problems[].name

flags.name: fail-on
flags.description: Exit 1 while incidents of this severity or worse are open: critical, warning or none

commands.name: status-pages
commands.short: Manage public status pages, their layout, posted incidents and subscribers
commands.long:
A status page is a public page that shows chosen monitors and manual rows
as components, under names you pick; a monitor's own name and target are
never shown. A page starts unpublished: set its layout, check it with a
preview link, then publish it. Changes to a published page, and incidents
posted on it, are public within a minute.

Pages are named by their id or exact slug. Any Norcube Monitor scope reads
them; a CI token changes them, posts on them or reaches their subscribers
only with the monitor.statuspages scope, which no other scope includes,
because what it changes is public and subscribers' addresses are personal
data.

commands.name: create
commands.short: Create a status page, unpublished
commands.long:
Creates a page that nobody can see yet: set what it shows with "layout
set", check it with "preview-link", then "publish" it. Every setting is
required: the page's public face is your choice, so nothing is filled in
for you. A boolean takes =false to turn it off. The one exception is
--auto-post, which is off unless you ask for it.

--auto-post lets the page post by itself: a monitor incident that stays
critical for 3 minutes is posted in fixed wording and emailed to subscribers,
and the post resolves when the incident does. A warning is never posted.

Your organization's limit sets how many pages it can have, published or not.
commands.example: norcube monitor status-pages create "Acme status" --slug acme --time-zone Europe/Prague --uptime-days 90 --history-days 90 --show-uptime-bars --show-uptime-percent --show-response-time=false --search-indexing

flags.description: Show each component's uptime percentage (--show-uptime-percent=false hides it)

commands.name: delete
commands.short: Delete a status page with its layout and posted incidents
commands.long:
Deletes the page and everything on it, takes it offline and gives up its
old addresses. The monitors it shows are not touched.
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages delete acme
norcube monitor status-pages delete 6e0f4b1a-2c3d-4e5f-8a9b-0c1d2e3f4a5b --yes

commands.short: Show a status page and its settings
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages get acme
norcube monitor status-pages get acme -o json --query url

commands.name: incidents
commands.short: Post incidents on a status page and keep them updated
commands.long:
A posted incident is what you tell the public: a title, an impact and a
series of updates. It is separate from a monitor's own incidents, which stay
internal; a post may link to them for your navigation, but those links are
never published.

While a post is open, the status it gives an affected component wins over
what the component's monitor says. A post with status resolved moves to the
page's history. On a published page everything here is public within a
minute.

A page with --auto-post also posts by itself. A person's correction or update
on such a post takes it over for good: the system leaves it alone from then
on, and it ends when you end it.

commands.name: create
commands.short: Post an incident on a status page; public within a minute on a published page
commands.long:
Posts an incident with its first update. On a published page it is public
within a minute: write it for your customers. It counts toward the page's
overall status while it is open, and --component sets what the page shows
for the components it affects.

--monitor-incident links the monitor incidents the post is about, for your
own navigation; the links are never published. --notify also emails the first
update to the page's subscribers.
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages incidents create acme --title "Elevated API errors" --status investigating --impact minor --message "We are looking into it."
norcube monitor status-pages incidents create acme --title "Checkout is down" --status identified --impact major --message-file update.txt --component "Checkout=major_outage" --started-at 20m --notify

commands.name: update
commands.short: Correct a posted incident; public within a minute on a published page
commands.long:
Corrects a post's title, impact, start or references, and changes only what
you pass. It adds no update and doesn't move the status: for that, use
"incidents updates create". --component replaces the affected components as
a whole. Resolved posts can be corrected too. On a published page a
correction is public within a minute.

norcube monitor status-pages incidents update acme 8c7d6e5f-4a3b-4c2d-9e1f-0a1b2c3d4e5f --title "Elevated API errors in Europe"
norcube monitor status-pages incidents update acme 8c7d6e5f-4a3b-4c2d-9e1f-0a1b2c3d4e5f --impact major --component "API=partial_outage"

commands.name: updates
commands.short: Add updates to a posted incident
commands.long:
Updates are the timeline of a posted incident: "incidents get" shows them,
and they can't be edited or removed.

commands.command: norcube monitor status-pages incidents updates create
commands.name: create
commands.short: Post an update on an incident; public within a minute on a published page
commands.long:
Adds an update to an open post. Its status becomes the post's; resolved ends
the post and moves it to the page's history, after which it takes no more
updates (post a new incident instead). On a published page the update is
public within a minute. --component replaces the affected components, and
--notify also emails the update to the page's subscribers.
commands.usage: norcube monitor status-pages incidents updates create <page> <incident> [flags]
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages incidents updates create acme 8c7d6e5f-4a3b-4c2d-9e1f-0a1b2c3d4e5f --status monitoring --message "A fix is rolling out."
norcube monitor status-pages incidents updates create acme 8c7d6e5f-4a3b-4c2d-9e1f-0a1b2c3d4e5f --status resolved --message "All clear." --notify

commands.name: layout
commands.short: Show or replace what a status page shows
commands.long:
A layout lists a page's components: first those outside any group, then the
groups, each in the order given. A component follows a monitor (kind
monitor, with the aspects that count: availability, certificate, domain)
or has a status you set (kind manual, with manualStatus operational,
degraded_performance, partial_outage or major_outage). The name is what
the public sees; the monitor's name and target never are.

commands.name: get
commands.short: Show a status page's layout
commands.long: -o json prints the document "layout set" takes, so you can edit and send it back.
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages layout get acme
norcube monitor status-pages layout get acme -o json > layout.json

commands.name: set
commands.short: Replace a status page's layout from a JSON file; public within a minute on a published page
commands.long:
Replaces the layout as a whole and prints the saved one. On a published page
the result is public within a minute, and adding a monitor publishes its
status, so you must be able to read every monitor you name.

The file has "components" and "groups" (use [] for none), in the shape
"layout get -o json" prints. Keep a row's id to keep the row, leave it out
for a new one. A row left out of the file is removed, and with it its place
on any posted incident.
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages layout set acme --file layout.json
norcube monitor status-pages layout get acme -o json | jq '.groups[0].collapsed = true' | norcube monitor status-pages layout set acme --file -

flags.name: file
flags.description: Read the layout as JSON from this file (- for standard input)

commands.name: list
commands.short: List status pages, newest first
commands.long:
Lists the organization's status pages, published or not. --monitor lists
the pages that show one monitor instead (at most 50, on one page).
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages list
norcube monitor status-pages list --monitor "Shop"
norcube monitor status-pages list -o json --query "[?published].url"

commands.name: preview-link
commands.short: Print a link to the rendered page that works for 15 minutes
commands.long:
Prints a signed link to the page as the public would see it, published or
not. Anyone with the link can open it until it expires, 15 minutes later,
so treat it like a draft you are sharing. It changes nothing, but a CI
token needs the monitor.statuspages scope to get one.
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages preview-link acme
norcube monitor status-pages preview-link acme -o text | cut -f1

commands.name: publish
commands.short: Make a status page public within a minute
commands.long:
Publishes the page at its address: it is public within a minute, along
with its page.json and its Atom feed. It needs at least one component.
Publishing a published page changes nothing.
commands.example: norcube monitor status-pages publish acme

commands.name: subscribers
commands.short: See and delete the people who get a status page's email updates
commands.long:
Subscribers are people who asked for email updates through the form on a
status page. An address stays pending until it confirms from the mail it
gets, and is removed if it hasn't after 7 days; only a confirmed address
gets updates. Every mail sent counts as an email notification in your
Norcube Monitor usage.

Updates reach subscribers when you post with --notify ("incidents create",
"incidents updates create") and when the page's --auto-post posts for you.

Addresses are personal data. Listing or deleting them takes the
monitor:ManageStatusPageSubscribers permission and, on a CI token, the
monitor.statuspages scope: no other scope reaches them, not even one that
reads the page itself.

commands.name: delete
commands.short: Delete a subscriber and any mail queued for them
commands.long:
Deletes the subscriber by id ("subscribers list" shows it) and any mail
queued for them. Their address isn't kept, so they can subscribe again.
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages subscribers delete acme 3f2a1b0c-9d8e-4f7a-b6c5-d4e3f2a1b0c9
norcube monitor status-pages subscribers delete acme 3f2a1b0c-9d8e-4f7a-b6c5-d4e3f2a1b0c9 --yes

flags.name: yes
flags.description: Don't ask for confirmation

commands.name: list
commands.short: List a status page's subscribers, newest first
commands.long:
Lists confirmed and pending subscribers. COMPONENTS is "all", or how many
of the page's components the subscriber follows; -o json has their ids.

The output holds personal data, so keep it out of build logs and other places
many people can read.
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages subscribers list acme
norcube monitor status-pages subscribers list acme --all-pages -o json --query "[?status=='confirmed'].email"

commands.name: unpublish
commands.short: Take a status page offline, keeping everything on it
commands.long:
The page's address stops answering and its old addresses are given up, so
another organization can take them. Its layout and posted incidents stay,
and preview links keep working. Unpublishing an unpublished page changes
nothing.
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages unpublish acme
norcube monitor status-pages unpublish acme --yes

commands.name: update
commands.short: Change a status page's address, texts or settings
commands.long:
Changes only what you pass. On a published page the change is public within
a minute.

--slug moves the page to a new address. The old address of a published
page redirects to the new one for 30 days, and no other organization can
take it meanwhile; unpublishing or deleting the page gives it up.

--auto-post=false stops new automatic posts; one already open still ends by
itself when its monitors recover.
commands.example:
norcube monitor status-pages update acme --name "Acme Inc. status"
norcube monitor status-pages update acme --slug acme-inc
norcube monitor status-pages update acme --uptime-days 30 --show-response-time
norcube monitor status-pages update acme --auto-post
